result.summary: Splits into a numerical-algorithm half (compact-WY recurrence, FP32-accurate mixed precision) and a GPU-implementation half (Triton and CuTe DSL on Blackwell sm_100, persistent per-matrix kernels for large-batch small-n), across five complementary angles.

results.title: ALAFF: Blocked Householder QR factorization (UT-FLAME)
results.snippet: Directly answers Deliverable 1 with code-level formulas in the exact packed (H,tau) form torch.geqrf returns. Gives the UT/WY transform Q = I - U·T^{-1}·U^H (equivalently I - U·S·U^H); builds the triangular factor as T = triu(U^H·U) with the diagonal SET to the tau coefficients τ₀..τ_{k-1}; and decomposes the trailing update (I - U·T^{-1}·U^H)·B into three GEMMs: W := U^H·B, then W := T^{-1}·W (triangular solve), then B := B - U·W. Storage convention is explicit: R_11 in the upper triangle of A_11, Householder vectors (implicit unit diagonal) below the diagonal, tau stored separately — i.e. the geqrf packed layout. This is the single best math-foundation reference.

results.title: LAPACK reference: DLARFT (form triangular factor T of a block reflector)
results.snippet: Canonical LAPACK routine the question names explicitly. Forms H = I - V·T·V^T from k elementary reflectors. With STOREV='C', reflector H(i) is stored in column i of V (column storage = the geqrf below-diagonal layout). Computes T via a Level-2 bordering recurrence: at step j the (j-1)x(j-1) upper-triangular T is bordered to jxj, with the new column built from tau(j) on the diagonal and the -tau(j)·V^T·V cross terms above. This is the authoritative source for the exact tau/T recurrence that produces the packed form; the column-storage variant is what maps to geqrf output.

results.title: LAPACK reference: DGEQRT3 (recursive compact-WY panel factorization)
results.snippet: Reference implementation of the recursive panel/T-matrix factorization (geqrt3) — the modern, GEMM-heavy way to do panel + T-build simultaneously. Directly relevant to Deliverable 2 (writing the tall-skinny panel factorization) and Deliverable 4 (one-matrix-per-threadblock blocked QR), because the divide-and-conquer recurrence turns the T construction itself into Level-3 BLAS, which is exactly what you want to map onto Triton/CuTe tensor-core GEMMs rather than the bordering Level-2 loop in DLARFT.

results.title: Elmroth & Gustavson — Applying recursion to serial and parallel QR factorization (IBM J. R&D)
results.snippet: The foundational paper behind DGEQRT3's recursive compact-WY scheme. Derives the recursive panel factorization and the recursive construction of the triangular T factor that lets the trailing update A := (I - V·T·V^T)·A be expressed almost entirely as matrix-matrix products. Provides the math justification for casting both panel factorization AND the T-build as tensor-core GEMMs on Blackwell, and explains the tau/reflector bookkeeping in the packed geqrf layout — central to Deliverables 1, 3 and 5.

results.title: Schreiber & Van Loan — A Storage-Efficient WY Representation for Products of Householder Transformations (SIAM J. Sci. Comput.)
results.snippet: The original derivation of the compact-WY ("storage-efficient WY") representation Q = I - Y·T·Y^T with Y unit-lower-trapezoidal and T kxk upper triangular. Establishes exactly why T is upper triangular and how it relates the individual reflectors and their tau scalars to a single blocked reflector — the theoretical basis the question asks for in Deliverable 1. Foundational and precise; pair with DLARFT for the implementable recurrence.

results.title: Kurzak & Dongarra — QR Factorization for the CELL Processor (LAPACK Working Note 201)
results.snippet: Walks through DGEQRT (panel + T), DLARFB (Level-3 trailing update I - V·T·V^T applied as a GEMM), and the tiled/blocked QR data flow on a manycore accelerator with small fast local memory — a close architectural analog to keeping a 512x512 factorization in B200 shared memory/registers (Deliverable 4). Useful as a worked blocked-kernel template and for understanding how panel and trailing-update kernels are scheduled, though precision and tcgen05 specifics are out of scope.

results.title: Recovering single precision accuracy from Tensor Cores while surpassing the FP32 theoretical peak performance (Ootomo & Yokota, 2022)
results.snippet: THE canonical reference for Deliverable 5. Splits each FP32 operand into two TF32/FP16 components plus a residual term and adds an error-correction step so a series of low-precision tensor-core MMAs reproduces EXACT FP32 accumulation accuracy. Achieves 33 TFlop/s full-FP32-exponent-range on A100 TF32 cores (vs 19.5 theoretical FP32 peak) and shows one of the three correction terms can be dropped (75% of TC work) with NO accuracy loss. This is the recipe for getting FP32-accurate (H,tau) out of TF32 trailing-update GEMMs. Released as the WMMAe-TCEC / tcec library (enp1s0.github.io). Directly answers whether split-float emulation reaches FP32 accuracy: yes, it matches FP32 SIMT cores bit-for-bit, so it survives the rtol=20·n·eps32 / 100·n·eps32 gates because the GEMM error is at FP32 level independent of conditioning.

results.title: [2.8] 3xTF32: FP32 accuracy with 2x Performance · NVIDIA/cutlass Discussion #361
results.snippet: Most directly actionable for the kernel author. NVIDIA's official writeup of the 3xTF32 algorithm: split each FP32 input into 3 TF32 chunks (big/medium/small), do 3 (not 9) TF32 tensor-core GEMMs and drop the lowest cross-terms, recovering near-FP32 accuracy at ~2x FP32 throughput. This is exactly the trailing-update (I−VTVᵀ)A GEMM strategy for the dominant batch=640/n=512 shape. Blackwell sm_100 tcgen05 retains TF32 paths, so the 3xTF32 emulation maps onto B200. Provides the error-vs-#splits tradeoff (1x/2x/3x TF32) needed to tune which trailing updates need full precision vs. can run cheaper. Pair with iterative refinement for the ill-conditioned cases.

results.title: Rounding Error Analysis of Mixed Precision Block Householder QR Algorithms (Yang, Fox, Sanders)
results.snippet: The decisive paper for whether mixed-precision Householder survives the accuracy gates. Gives backward-error and orthogonality bounds for BLOCK (compact-WY) Householder QR when the panel and trailing GEMM run in reduced precision. Key result the contract demands: Householder QR's orthogonality error ||QᵀQ−I|| is bounded by a low-degree polynomial in n times the working-precision unit roundoff and is essentially INDEPENDENT of condition number (unlike CholeskyQR, which scales with κ²). Establishes which operations (the reflector inner products, the T-matrix build) must stay FP32 and which (trailing-update GEMM) tolerate TF32 — exactly the split needed for rank-deficient/clustered-singular-value inputs.

results.title: Mixed precision iterative refinement for least squares (Gao, Ma, Shao, 2025; NLAA)
results.snippet: Defines the condition-number ceiling for Deliverable 5/6. Shows a low-precision QR can be refined back to working precision, BUT the hard limit: if QR is done in fp16, LS iterative refinement only converges for κ∞ ≲ 4.88×10⁴; beyond that you need GMRES-based IR with the QR factors as a preconditioner. Critical for the contract's ill-conditioned/near-rank-deficient inputs: it tells you a single low-precision pass will FAIL the residual gate on the hard matrices, and quantifies when a correction sweep (extra GEMM in higher precision) rescues it. Informs the 'refinement' branch of the ranked approach list and its risk.

results.title: Ozaki Scheme II: GEMM-oriented FP emulation via integer modular technique (Uchino, Ozaki, Imamura, 2025)
results.snippet: The INT8-tensor-core alternative to 3xTF32 for FP32-accurate GEMM, relevant to Deliverable 5's emulation menu. Splits operands into integer slices computed exactly on INT8 matrix engines (ozIMMU), with a tunable #slices that trades accuracy for speed. Key caveat for this problem: 7-8 slices needed even for well-conditioned data, and the required slice count GROWS with matrix conditioning (ϕ parameter) — so on the contract's ill-conditioned inputs the INT8/Ozaki path gets expensive fast, making 3xTF32 + Householder (condition-independent) generally the better bet for the trailing update. Useful as a reference point and a fallback when even tighter-than-FP32 accuracy is wanted on B200 INT8 cores.

results.title: Shifted CholeskyQR for computing the QR factorization of ill-conditioned matrices (Fukaya et al.)
results.snippet: Directly addresses the contract's warning that 'naive CholeskyQR that squares the condition number will FAIL.' Explains why CholeskyQR2 has a prohibitive κ restriction and how a diagonal shift (shifted CholeskyQR3) restores stability at ~50% extra cost — a cheaper-than-Householder panel option for the batched tall-skinny factorization IF conditioning is bounded. Relevant to Deliverable 6 as a distinct candidate approach (fast Cholesky-based panel + shift + refinement) versus pure Householder, with the explicit risk that the contract's rank-deficient/clustered cases may exceed even the shifted method's stable range, so it must be guarded by a residual check / Householder fallback.

results.title: FlashRNN: I/O-Aware Optimization of Traditional RNNs on modern hardware
results.snippet: Most directly on-point for Deliverable 2's Triton-expressibility question. States the hard constraint verbatim: 'there is no (grid) synchronization between programs in Triton, which makes it impossible to communicate values between different programs over HBM.' This is exactly why a QR panel's sequential top-to-bottom dependency cannot be split across Triton programs — the entire panel + its trailing update must live inside ONE program (one matrix per program/threadblock), with shared memory and the compiler-inserted intra-block barriers as the only sync. The paper also works through the consequence for register/shared-memory budgets and head-dimension limits, which is the same occupancy reasoning that bounds a per-matrix QR megakernel on B200. Confirms the persistent-one-program-per-matrix design is the right Triton shape for the small-n large-batch regime.

results.title: Persistent Matmul — Triton documentation (09-persistent-matmul.py)
results.snippet: The canonical, copy-pasteable Triton persistent-kernel reference for the trailing-update GEMM (A := (I − VTVᵀ)A) and for the one-program-per-SM/per-matrix loop structure. Shows naive vs persistent vs TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) matmul variants and how the persistent loop keeps a fixed grid of programs alive, each pulling tiles of work — the exact scaffold for issuing hundreds of independent batch=640/n=512 factorizations or fusing panel+update without re-launch overhead. Docs note Hopper/Blackwell get the most benefit from the persistent API + block-pointer/TMA abstractions because of their async memory pipelines, which is relevant to sm_100. Source file: triton/python/tutorials/09-persistent-matmul.py.

results.title: 3D tensor tl.dot() Assertion `idx < size()' failed — triton-lang/triton Issue #5243
results.snippet: Concrete evidence of what tl.dot can and cannot express — load-bearing for deciding whether a batched QR can use a single 3D batched tl.dot or must loop per-matrix. Documents a real failure with 3D (batched) tl.dot operands, reinforcing that Triton's tensor-core dot is fundamentally a 2D MMA: minimum block 16x16, dims multiples of 16 (so n=32 panels are near the granularity floor and the batch dimension cannot be folded into the contraction). For the trailing-update GEMM and panel inner products this means one program processes one matrix's 2D tiles; batching is expressed by the grid/program axis, not inside tl.dot. tl.dot lowers to mma.sync (Tensor Core) when shapes are compatible.

results.title: Batch QR Factorization on GPUs: Design, Optimization, and Tuning (ICCS 2022, Dongarra et al.)
results.snippet: The most directly transferable algorithm/design source for the large-batch small/medium-n regime (Deliverable 4), even though it's CUDA not Triton — it tells you what a Triton per-matrix kernel must reproduce. Details the MAGMA-style batched geqrf: one threadblock per matrix, panel factorized in registers/shared memory up to the threadblock thread limit, then subsequent panels load the triangular T factor into shared memory and apply the compact-WY trailing update; assigning b operations per threadblock to keep occupancy when matrices are small; and the shared-memory (N×N) ceiling on occupancy (worse in FP64 than FP32 — relevant since the contract demands FP32 output). Pairs the blocked Householder recurrence with the one-block-per-matrix mapping the Triton design needs.

results.title: Batched one-sided factorizations of tiny matrices using GPUs: Challenges and countermeasures
results.snippet: Directly addresses the smallest scored shapes (n=32, and the register-vs-shared crossover for n=176/352). Enumerates the countermeasures for batching thousands of tiny Householder factorizations: optimal memory traffic, register blocking, and concurrency control; states the key design rule that register-resident factorization wins for very small matrices but you must switch to shared-memory-based kernels at larger n to keep occupancy. This is the occupancy/register-limit reasoning Deliverable 4 asks for, and it maps cleanly onto choosing whether each Triton program keeps the matrix in registers or shared memory on B200's 228 KB/SM budget.

results.title: Mirage Persistent Kernel: A Compiler and Runtime for Mega-Kernelizing Tensor Programs
results.snippet: Supports the 'single persistent megakernel vs a sequence of batched-GEMM launches' decision (Deliverable 4/6). Describes fusing many sequential operators into one persistent GPU kernel by decomposing into tasks and minimizing inter-level data movement, eliminating per-call launch overhead and maximizing on-chip residency — exactly the tradeoff for a fused panel+trailing-update QR megakernel versus iterated cuBLAS-style batched GEMMs. Useful as evidence that the megakernel approach is a recognized, compiler-supported pattern, and for the task-graph framing of the QR panel→update sequential dependency.

results.title: Batch QR Factorization on GPUs: Design, Optimization, and Tuning (Abdelfattah, Tomov, Dongarra — ICCS 2022)
results.snippet: THE single most on-target reference for Deliverables 1 and 4. Spells out the MAGMA blocked Householder design exactly: nested blocking where a wide panel is internally sub-blocked, the unblocked dgeqr2 panel done one column at a time, then the trailing update A=(I−VTVᵀ)A applied as L3 batch GEMM (Q=I−V·T·Vᵀ). Gives both forms of the compact-WY T-matrix recurrence in pseudocode (T1:nb,1:nb = Vᵀ·V then per-column −τj·T·…). Panel kernel maps ONE THREAD PER ROW and caches the m×nb panel in the REGISTER FILE; nb must be a compile-time constant to avoid register spilling and is instantiated for 1≤nb≤nbmax. Documents the exact occupancy cliff: a 512×nb panel needs 512 threads → max 4 thread blocks/SM (hardware limit), and panels taller than 512 cause ≥25% occupancy drop — directly relevant to the n=512/1024/2048/4096 scored shapes. Proposes a SECOND shared-memory panel kernel (nb ≤ #threads ≤ m) when the register/thread-per-row version runs out of occupancy, with offline autotuning over panel width/precision/arch to pick register-vs-smem at runtime. Multi-level kernel fusion of the dgeqr2 building blocks gives 12.9–57.1% (square) / 11.9–41.4% (tall-skinny) gains; final up to 3.22× vs best competition, 16.2×/25.4× (SP/DP) vs cuBLAS. Key insight: only MAGMA calls batch GEMM underneath, so it scales while cuBLAS/KBLAS stagnate — confirms the panel+batched-GEMM structure is what wins at the dominant 640×512 shape.

results.title: Batched one-sided factorizations of tiny matrices using GPUs: Challenges and countermeasures (Abdelfattah, Haidar, Tomov, Dongarra — J. Comp. Sci. 2018)
results.snippet: THE reference for the small-n large-batch regime (Deliverable 4) — matrices of size 32 and less, millions of them, which maps to the scored 20×32 and 40×176/352 shapes. Establishes the core design axes for one-matrix-per-threadblock factorization: (1) 1D vs 2D thread config (1D gives ~10.5×/9.6× over 2D for Cholesky); (2) matrix storage in register file vs shared memory with the whole matrix kept in one or the other for the entire factorization — registers faster but power-of-2-size constrained, shared memory more flexible but N×N smem footprint limits occupancy; QR specifically uses HYBRID storage (registers for the matrix + shared-memory or warp-shuffle communication for reductions), which beats pure-smem. (3) CONCURRENCY CONTROL — the key trick for tiny n: since an 8×8 matrix only needs an (8,1) block that wastes a warp and the runtime caps at 32 TBs/SM, they aggregate nFTB matrices into one block via an (8,nFTB) config; with nFTB=4 you factorize 128 matrices/SM instead of 32 → 4× speedup, valid as long as register/smem can host them. nFTB is a runtime-tunable parameter (autotuned 1–16; no gain beyond) and doesn't help for n>16 because hardware rounds threads up to a full warp anyway. Reports up to 11.8× vs cuBLAS on V100. This is the playbook for packing hundreds of independent small QRs into persistent threadblocks in registers/shared memory.

results.title: Batched QR and SVD algorithms on GPUs with applications in hierarchical matrix compression (Boukaram, Turkiyyah, Ltaief, Keyes — Parallel Computing 2018, KBLAS)
results.snippet: The KBLAS counterpart to MAGMA's batched QR/SVD — the 'other' state-of-the-art batched factorization design the 2022 paper benchmarks against. Relevant to Deliverable 4 as a contrasting per-threadblock approach: KBLAS keeps the whole small matrix resident in fast memory and is competitive (sometimes ahead of MAGMA) on tall-skinny shapes precisely because there the trailing update is NOT rich in batch GEMM. Useful for understanding when a self-contained one-block kernel beats a panel+batched-GEMM decomposition, and as a real-world driver (hierarchical/H-matrix compression) for exactly the hundreds-of-small-QRs workload. Abstract-only on ScienceDirect; the algorithmic detail overlaps with the two ICL papers above.

results.title: cuSOLVERDx — geqrf (device-side QR factorization, CUDA-X math library)
results.snippet: NVIDIA's modern device-side answer to 'batched small QR': cuSOLVERDx exposes geqrf as a DEVICE function you call from inside your own CUDA kernel, so you can run one factorization per threadblock and FUSE it with surrounding work — exactly the one-matrix-per-threadblock pattern Deliverable 4 asks about, but vendor-provided. Confirms the (H,tau) packed output contract (reflectors below the diagonal + tau array represent Q as a product of min(M,N) Householder vectors), matching torch.geqrf. Although the task says don't recommend library calls as the answer, cuSOLVERDx is the closest reference implementation for the threadblock-resident design and a useful performance baseline; the docs also indicate the shared-memory/register sizing the device routine needs, informing the B200 228KB-smem budget question. Header-only, Blackwell-capable.

results.title: Efficient GPU-Centered Singular Value Decomposition Using the Householder QR (arXiv 2508.11467, 2025)
results.snippet: Recent (2025) GPU-centered SVD built on Householder QR — closest in time to the B200/sm_100 target. Relevant secondarily: it reuses a batched/GPU-resident Householder QR as its workhorse and discusses keeping the factorization on-GPU to avoid host round-trips, which echoes the 'persistent megakernel vs sequence of batched-GEMM calls' question. Less directly about the large-batch small-n packing than the two ICL papers, and framed around SVD rather than the bare geqrf (H,tau) contract, so use as supplementary modern context rather than a primary recipe.

claims.claim: The compact-WY block reflector that aggregates a panel of Householder reflectors is given exactly by H = I - V*T*V^T, where V holds the reflector vectors in unit-lower-triangular form and T is an N-by-N upper triangular matrix; this is the trailing-update operator the research question needs to map to tensor-core GEMMs.
claims.quote: The block reflector H is then given by H = I - V * T * V**T where V**T is the transpose of V.

claims.claim: The recursive panel factorization natively produces the torch.geqrf-style packed form: on exit, the elements on and above the diagonal of A hold the N-by-N upper triangular R, and the elements below the diagonal hold the reflector vectors V (with the unit diagonal not stored) — exactly the (H) packing the problem contract requires.
claims.quote: The elements on and above the diagonal contain the N-by-N upper triangular matrix R; the elements below the diagonal are the columns of V.

claims.claim: The off-diagonal block T3 of the composite T factor for two stacked panels is computed as T3 = -T1 * (Y1^H * Y2) * T2, giving the full block structure T = [[T1, T3],[0, T2]]; this is the exact recurrence for assembling the T matrix from two sub-panels.
claims.quote: Compute T3 = T(1:N1,J1:N) = -T1 Y1^H Y2 T2

claims.claim: DGEQRT3 is a recursive (divide-and-conquer) compact-WY panel QR algorithm that splits the N columns into a left half N1=N/2 and right half N2, recurses on each, applies Q1^T to the right block, and merges — demonstrating that the panel factorization itself can be cast as recursive GEMM-heavy work rather than a strictly sequential column loop.
claims.quote: DGEQRT3 recursively computes a QR factorization of a real M-by-N matrix A, using the compact WY representation of Q.

claims.claim: The recursive compact-WY algorithm implemented here is the Elmroth and Gustavson method, providing a citable algorithmic foundation for the blocked/recursive QR the research question asks to reproduce.
claims.quote: Based on the algorithm of Elmroth and Gustavson, IBM J. Res. Develop. Vol 44 No. 4 July 2000.

claims.claim: A product of r Householder matrices Q = P_1...P_r (each m x m) can be written in the compact-WY form Q = I + Y*T*Y^T, where Y is m x r and T is r x r upper triangular. This is the exact representation that blocked Householder QR (and the geqrf packed H/tau form) accumulates, and the single dense Y*T*Y^T product is what maps the trailing update A := (I - V*T*V^T)*A onto a tensor-core GEMM.
claims.quote: the matrix Q can be expressed in the form Q = I + YTY^T, where Y ∈ R^(m × r) and T ∈ R^(r × r) with T upper triangular

claims.claim: The compact form using (Y, T) is more storage-efficient than the original two-matrix WY form because the r x r upper-triangular T replaces the second m x r W matrix; with r << m the compact representation costs r(m+r) elements versus 2mr. This matters for keeping a per-matrix factorization resident in B200 shared memory / registers for the large-batch small-n regime.
claims.quote: Usually r ≪ m and so this 'compact' WY representation requires less storage

claims.claim: The entire motivation for the WY / compact-WY representation is to recast the QR update from matrix-vector (level-2 BLAS) operations into matrix-matrix (level-3 BLAS) operations, which is precisely the transformation needed to feed the trailing-update as a tensor-core GEMM on Blackwell.
claims.quote: high-performance computing environments that are especially good at matrix-matrix multiplication

claims.claim: Against the competing block-reflector strategy of Schreiber and Parlett, the compact-WY (I + YTY^T) representation retains a storage advantage while requiring a comparable amount of arithmetic work, so adopting the T-matrix form does not increase the FLOP count of the blocked QR.
claims.quote: the new technique still has a storage advantage and involves a comparable amount of work

H_{k-1} = I - U T^{-1} U^H, where U holds the Householder vectors and T is upper triangular. This is exactly the accumulated form needed to express the trailing update as matrix-matrix products and is the algebraic basis for the packed (H, tau) layout that torch.geqrf returns.
claims.quote: If \(H_0, \cdots , H_{k-1}\) are Householder transformations, then \(H_0 H_1 \cdots H_{k-1} = I - U T^{-1} U^H\)

claims.claim: The block triangular factor T is computed as the upper-triangular part of U^H U, with the diagonal then divided by two OR set to the tau coefficients tau_0,...,tau_{k-1}. This gives a concrete, GEMM-friendly recipe (a single U^H U product plus a diagonal fix-up) to build T from the panel's Householder vectors and tau values — directly relevant to forming the T matrix on tensor cores.
claims.quote: T = \triu( U^H U ) (the upper triangular part of U^H U) followed by either dividing the diagonal elements by two or setting them to \tau_0 , \ldots, \tau_{k-1} (in order).

claims.claim: Applying the accumulated transform to the trailing block factors into three matrix-matrix operations: W := U^H B (GEMM), W := T^{-1} W (triangular solve), then B := B - U W (GEMM), via the identity (I - U T^{-1} U^H) B = B - U(T^{-1}(U^H B)). This is precisely how the trailing update maps onto tensor-core GEMMs.
claims.quote: (I - UT⁻¹Uᴴ)B = B - U(T⁻¹(UᴴB))

claims.claim: The blocked QR algorithm's trailing update for a column panel is W_12 = T_11^{-H}(U_11^H A_12 + U_21^H A_22), followed by A_12 := A_12 - U_11 W_12 and A_22 := A_22 - U_21 W_12 — giving the exact panel-trailing recurrence (factor panel via unblocked QR, FormT, then GEMM update) for a blocked implementation.

Blocking casts most of the QR computation as matrix-matrix multiplication (BLAS-3), which performs O(m^3) work on O(m^2) data and therefore reuses data, whereas unblocked Householder QR is dominated by lower-order BLAS-2 operations with no reuse — the rationale for why a GEMM-bound (tensor-core) trailing update is the path to performance.
claims.quote: Matrix-matrix multiplication performs O(m³) computation with O(m²) data, and hence there is an opportunity to reuse data

claims.claim: Tile QR decomposes the factorization into four computational kernels (LAPACK-style names SGEQRT, STSQRT, SLARFB, SSSRFB) that operate on small square tiles; SGEQRT factors a diagonal tile producing R, a unit-lower-triangular V of Householder reflectors, AND the compact-WY upper-triangular T matrix (stored separately), so the algorithm natively produces the V/tau-style reflector representation rather than an explicit Q. This maps directly onto the research question's per-tile panel + trailing-GEMM structure.
claims.quote: The algorithm relies on four basic operations implemented by four computational kernels (Figure 1). ... SGEQRT: The kernel performs the QR factorization of a diagonal tile of the input matrix and produces an upper triangular matrix R and a unit lower triangular matrix V containing the Householder reflectors. The kernel also produces the upper triangular matrix T as defined by the compact WY technique for accumulating Householder reflectors [19, 20]. ... The R factor overrides the upper triangular portion of the input and the reflectors override the lower triangular portion of the input. The T matrix is stored separately.

claims.claim: The compact-WY representation lets the trailing update be expressed as level-3 BLAS (GEMM): it requires one T matrix of size equal to the panel width per panel, and the overhead of manipulating T is negligible because T is much smaller than the panel height. This is exactly the (I − VTVᵀ)A → tensor-core GEMM mapping the research question asks about, with its cost amortization condition.
claims.quote: LAPACK-style block QR factorization relies on the compact WY technique for accumulating Householder reflectors in order to express computation in terms of level 3 BLAS (matrix-vector) operations. The technique requires calculation of a square matrix T per each panel of the input matrix, where the size of T is equal to the width of the panel and, most of the time, much smaller than the height of the panel. In this case, the overhead associated with manipulating the T matrices is negligible.

claims.claim: There is a quantified extra-flops vs memory-intensity tradeoff: naive per-tile T construction (one T per square tile) costs ~25% more operations than standard QR, while a pure level-2-BLAS update has the same flop count as standard QR (2MN² − 2/3 N³) but performs poorly because it is memory-bound. The performance sweet spot is inner-blocking inside the tile, with T stored as triangular blocks of the inner block size on the diagonal. This directly informs block-size choice for the trailing-update GEMM strategy.
claims.quote: In a naive implementation of the tile QR factorization, a T matrix is produced for each square tile of the panel and used in updating tiles to the right of each tile of the panel. This approach results in 25 % more operations than the standard QR algorithm. ... in such case, the updating algorithm results in the same number of floating point operations as the standard QR algorithm (2MN² −2/3N³). Obviously, such implementation has to perform poorly due to the memory-bound nature of level 2 BLAS. The key to achieving performance is to find the right trade-off between extra operations and memory intensity.

claims.claim: On the CELL processor (a SIMD many-core analogous in spirit to a GPU SM array), a 512×512 single-precision tile-QR factorization ran in 1645 µs at 109 Gflop/s (53% of peak, 62% of the trailing-update kernel's peak), and the implementation crossed half of peak performance for problems as small as 512×512. This is a concrete reference data point for the research question's dominant 512×512 shape, showing tiled Householder QR (not CholeskyQR) is the path and that small-n tiled QR can reach a meaningful fraction of peak.
claims.quote: Figure 5: Execution trace of a factorization of a 512×512 matrix. (total time: 1645 µs, execution rate: 109 Gflop/s). ... The presented implementation crosses half of the peak performance for problems as small as 512×512.

claims.claim: The panel factorization (production of a block of reflectors) is small and sequential enough to be executed entirely in the register file as fully unrolled straight-line code: a 64×4 reflector block was produced using 64 registers by loading the panel once, performing the steps (one reflector produced and applied to the rest of the panel each step), then storing — but this register-resident straight-line panel alone was insufficient for peak, requiring the trailing update (apply-to-trailing-submatrix) to also be heavily unrolled and special-cased. This supports the research question's per-warp/per-threadblock register-resident unblocked-Householder panel design for the large-batch small-n regime.
claims.quote: at each step (each outer loop iteration), a block of reflectors of the same size is produced (64×4). This allows for performing the panel factorization (production of four reflectors) to be executed entirely in the register file, using 64 registers. First, the panel is loaded, then four steps are performed, each producing one reflector and applying it to the rest of the panel, then the panel is stored. The whole procedure is completely unrolled to one block of straight-line code. As extreme as it might seem, this step alone proves to be insufficient to deliver the desired performance.

claims.claim: 3xTF32 (a CUTLASS algorithm using Ampere tensor cores to emulate FP32) matches the accuracy of a native FP32 instruction while delivering at least 2x throughput.
claims.quote: Using Ampere tensor cores to emulate FP32 operations, 3xTF32 matches the accuracy of FP32 instruction with at least 2x throughput.

claims.claim: 3xTF32 is an emulation technique: FP32 GEMM accuracy is approximated by composing multiple TF32 tensor-core operations rather than executing native FP32 on tensor cores, establishing the feasibility of FP32-accurate results on TF32 hardware (relevant to the QR trailing-update GEMM precision requirement).
claims.quote: Using Ampere tensor cores to emulate FP32 operations

claims.claim: The Ozaki Scheme II uses INT8 tensor cores with integer modular arithmetic (Chinese Remainder Theorem) to emulate FP64-accuracy GEMM, achieving 56.6-80.2 TFLOPS FP64-equivalent on GH200 and exceeding native FP64 tensor core throughput (61.9 TFLOPS). This shows the trailing-update GEMM in blocked QR could be done at FP64-level accuracy on low-precision (INT8) tensor cores, but at a multiplication-count cost.
claims.quote: The proposed method achieved 56.6–80.2 TFLOPS in FP64-equivalent precision on the GH200, and 7.4–9.8 TFLOPS on the RTX 4090.

claims.claim: Achieving DGEMM (FP64) accuracy via the modular Ozaki scheme requires 14-18 matrix multiplications (e.g. 14-15 moduli for phi=0.5; s=16 gives k=53 bits with 16 matmuls), which is a large constant-factor overhead. For an FP32-accurate (not FP64) QR target needing only ~24 bits of mantissa, far fewer splits/moduli would be needed, but the method's cost scales with the precision demanded.
claims.quote: For φ=0.5, both proposed methods require 14 or 15 moduli to achieve the accuracy of the DGEMM level.

claims.claim: INT8 tensor cores are theoretically 2x-4x faster than FP16 tensor cores, and the integer products A'_iB'_i are error-free (exactly representable in INT32) when q<2^17 via cublasGemmEx, making INT8 a viable substrate for exact/high-precision accumulation. On B200, where INT8 throughput vastly exceeds FP32, this is the relevant lever for emulating FP32-accurate GEMM on the dominant n=512 trailing update.
claims.quote: The first advantage of using INT8 TCs is that it is theoretically twice or 4x as fast as FP16 TCs.

claims.claim: The paper provides B200 (Blackwell) hardware specifications (40 TFLOPS FP64 tensor core in Table 1) but reports NO experimental results on B200 or any Blackwell GPU — all measurements are on GH200 (Hopper) and RTX 4090 (Ada). Performance of this emulation scheme on sm_100/tcgen05 5th-gen tensor cores is therefore unvalidated and must be extrapolated.
claims.quote: specifications for the H100 and GH200 are the same as those for the H200

claims.claim: The Ozaki Scheme II paper addresses ONLY matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM) and does not develop or discuss QR factorization or broader numerical linear algebra; it is useful to this QR research only as the GEMM-emulation building block for the trailing-update step, not as an end-to-end factorization method. Prior Ozaki-scheme work has been integrated into HPL/LINPACK, suggesting LA applicability but not demonstrated here for QR.
claims.quote: The potential applications of the Ozaki scheme are explored (Dawson et al., [2024])...its integration into the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark is demonstrated (Dongarra et al., [2024]).

claims.claim: An error-correction technique (retaining the mantissa lost during FP16/TF32 conversion in additional half-precision variables and using them in correction GEMMs) makes Tensor Core matrix multiplication EXACTLY match FP32 SIMT-core accuracy. This is the core viability proof for using TF32/BF16 tensor cores in the QR trailing-update GEMM while keeping final FP32 accuracy (research Q5/Q1).
claims.quote: we develop a high accuracy, high performance, and low power consumption matrix-matrix multiplication implementation using Tensor Cores, which exactly matches the accuracy of FP32 SIMT Cores while achieving superior throughput.

claims.claim: The FP32-emulation-on-tensor-cores approach beats the FP32 SIMT theoretical peak: 33 TFlop/s for the full FP32 exponent range via TF32 tensor cores and 51 TFlop/s (limited exponent range) via FP16 tensor cores, versus 19.5 TFlop/s FP32 SIMT peak on A100. This quantifies the speed payoff of routing the trailing GEMM through split-precision tensor cores rather than FP32 CUDA cores (Q5/Q3).
claims.quote: Our implementation achieves 51TFlop/s for a limited exponent range using FP16 Tensor Cores and 33TFlop/s for full exponent range of FP32 using TF32 Tensor Cores on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, which outperforms the theoretical FP32 SIMT Core peak performance of 19.5TFlop/s.

claims.claim: The naive single-correction split is INSUFFICIENT to reach FP32 accuracy; matching FP32 requires correctly handling rounding inside the Tensor Core and the underflow probability during the correction computation. This is the key implementation risk/caveat when applying the technique to ill-conditioned/rank-deficient QR inputs that must pass rtol=20*n*eps32 (Q5/Q6).
claims.quote: the correcting capability of this method alone is limited, and the resulting accuracy cannot match that of a matrix multiplication on FP32 SIMT Cores... the key to achieving this accuracy is how to deal with the rounding inside Tensor Cores and underflow probability during the correction computation.

claims.claim: The high-accuracy FP32-emulation GEMM is implemented on top of NVIDIA CUTLASS, establishing CUTLASS/CuTe as the vehicle for emulated-FP32 tensor-core GEMM kernels — directly relevant to using CUTLASS CuTe DSL for the QR trailing update (Q3).
claims.quote: The implementation is based on NVIDIA's CUTLASS.

claims.claim: The motivating applications are scientific-computing kernels (preconditioners for iterative solvers, low-precision Fourier transforms), not just ML; the paper does NOT directly address QR factorization, so its FP32-recovery guarantee is for GEMM and must be re-validated for the QR-specific orthogonality residual.
claims.quote: many applications in scientific computing such as preconditioners for iterative solvers and low-precision Fourier transforms can exploit these Tensor Cores.

claims.claim: Low-precision factorization combined with mixed-precision iterative refinement can refine a lower-precision solution back up to the working precision for least-squares-type problems, validating the general feasibility of using TF32/BF16 tensor-core factorization while recovering FP32 accuracy.
claims.quote: mixed precision techniques are capable of refining the lower precision solution to the working precision

claims.claim: Mixed-precision iterative refinement converges only when the factorization precision times the condition number of the (augmented) system stays bounded near unity (u_f·κ ≲ 1); this is the binding limit on how aggressively low precision can be used on ill-conditioned inputs.
claims.quote: For matrices A and B satisfying 𝒖_f·κ_∞(F̃)≲1, the limiting relative forward error is derived as [given bound]

claims.claim: For ill-conditioned matrices the standard refinement loop may diverge, and a GMRES-based correction solver (GMRES-IR) using the low-precision solution as an initial guess is required to restore convergence — relevant to handling the ill-conditioned/near-rank-deficient cases in the QR problem contract.
claims.quote: For ill-conditioned matrices, however, this approach may fail to converge. Therefore...applies a GMRES solver, capable of utilizing the lower precision solution as the initial guess.

claims.claim: Computing the residual in higher-than-working precision (u_r ≪ u) lets the refined solution achieve accuracy beyond the working precision, with limiting forward error bounded by 4(m+n+p+1)·cond(F̃,ũ)·u_r + u.

The mixed-precision factorization-and-refinement scheme reduces execution time by roughly 40% on average versus fixed (uniform) precision for reasonably well-conditioned problems — a quantitative speedup estimate for the low-precision-factorization-plus-refinement strategy.
claims.quote: our algorithms reduce the execution time by a factor of 40% on average compared to the fixed precision ones

claims.claim: A persistent Triton matmul kernel sizes its grid to the number of SMs (rather than one program per output tile), launching min(NUM_SMS, total_tiles) programs each of which loops over multiple tiles. This is the structural pattern needed for a persistent one-program-per-matrix batched QR megakernel on B200.
claims.quote: grid = lambda META: (min(NUM_SMS, triton.cdiv(M, META["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]) * triton.cdiv(N, META["BLOCK_SIZE_N"])), )

claims.claim: The number of SMs is queried at runtime from device properties and used to drive the persistent grid, so a batched-QR persistent kernel can size itself to the B200's SM count programmatically.
claims.quote: NUM_SMS = torch.cuda.get_device_properties("cuda").multi_processor_count

claims.claim: Within each persistent program, tiles are iterated via a strided tl.range loop (start_pid, num_tiles, NUM_SMS), so a single program processes a sequence of work items instead of idling after one tile — the mechanism by which one program can own multiple independent matrices in the large-batch regime.
claims.quote: for tile_id in tl.range(start_pid, num_tiles, NUM_SMS, flatten=True)

claims.claim: Triton exposes warp specialization through a flag on tl.range (warp_specialize), but it is Blackwell-only — on older GPUs it falls back to software pipelining; this is a Blackwell/sm_100-specific Triton capability relevant to B200 kernels.
claims.quote: This only works on Blackwell right now. On older GPUs, this will use software pipelining.

claims.claim: TMA tensor descriptors in Triton require compute capability >= 9.0 (Hopper and up), available both host-side (TensorDescriptor.from_tensor) and device-side (tl.make_tensor_descriptor); B200 (sm_100) satisfies this, so TMA-backed tile loads are usable for the trailing-update GEMM.
claims.quote: supports_tma(): return is_cuda() and torch.cuda.get_device_capability()[0] >= 9

claims.claim: The storage-efficient compact-WY representation factors Q = Q1Q2...Qk = I − YTY^T, where Y is m×k lower trapezoidal holding the k Householder vectors (each with an implicit leading 1, scaled by tau_i) and T is a k×k upper triangular matrix; this is exactly the packed (H, tau) form torch.geqrf returns, so the blocked algorithm natively produces it. For k=2, T = [[tau1, −tau1·u1^T·u2·tau2],[0, tau2]].
claims.quote: Later on, Schreiber and Van Loan, in [4], introduced a storageefficient WY representation for Q: Q ⫽ Q1Q2 · · · Qk ⫽ I ⫺ YTY T, (10) where T is an upper triangular k by k matrix. ... In (9) and (10) Y is a trapezoidal matrix consisting of k consecutive Householder vectors, ui, i ⫽ 1, . . . , k. The first component of each ui is 1, where the 1 is implicit and hence is not stored. These vectors are scaled with taui. For k ⫽ 2, the T of Equation (10) is T⫽ (tau1, 0; ⫺tau1 u1^T u2 tau2, tau2)

claims.claim: The T matrix for a split k = k1 + k2 is built by the block formula T = [[T1, −T1·(Y1^T·Y2)·T2],[0, T2]], where T1, T2 are the triangular factors of the two sub-blocks and Y=(Y1,Y2) is concatenation. This off-diagonal coupling block −T1(Y1^T Y2)T2 is computed entirely by GEMM (Y1^T·Y2) and two TRMM operations, giving a Level-3 (matrix–matrix) construction of T instead of LAPACK DLARFT's Level-2 bordering.
claims.quote: Thus, a generalization of (11) is T⫽ (T1, ⫺T1 Y1^T Y2 T2; 0, T2), (13) which is essentially a Level 3 formulation of (11), (12). ... as (12) and (13) suggest, Q ⫽ I ⫺ YTYT can be done recursively as a series of k ⫺ 1 matrix–matrix computations. ... The k1 k2 (2m ⫺ k1) FLOP component is the cost of computing ⫺T1(Y1^T Y2)T2

claims.claim: The trailing-matrix update applying Q^T = I − Y·T^T·Y^T to a block C (i.e. Ĉ = Q^T C = C − Y·T^T·(Y^T·C)) is implemented as a fixed sequence of six Level-3 BLAS calls — two TRMM (with the unit-triangular top block Y1), two GEMM (with the rectangular bottom block Y2), one TRMM by T^T, and a matrix subtract — for a total of kn(4m−k−1) FLOPs; partitioning Y=[Y1;Y2] with Y1 k×k unit lower triangular and Y2 (m−k)×k. This is the routine the paper calls DQTC (equivalent to LAPACK DLARFB).
claims.quote: The routine DQTC described in the next two subsections applies Q T ⫽ I ⫺ YT^T Y^T to a matrix C as a series of DGEMM and DTRMM operations. ... Table 1 ... DTRMM W ⫽ Y1^T * C1 ... DGEMM W ⫽ W ⫹ Y2^T * C2 ... DTRMM W ⫽ T^T * W ... DGEMM C2 ⫽ C2 ⫺ Y2 * W ... DTRMM W ⫽ C1 * W ... Matrix subtract C1 ⫽ C1 ⫺ W ... Total computation C ⫽ Q^T C kn(4m ⫺ k ⫺ 1)

claims.claim: Among five mathematically-equivalent orderings of the update Ĉ = C − Y·T^T·Y^T·C, method C1 = C − Y·[T^T·(Y^T·C)] has the lowest FLOP count (kn2(4n1−k−1)) for the typical QR case where the panel is tall (n1 large) and the block size k is small, and is therefore the ordering LAPACK DLARFB and the paper's DQTC both implement. Operand association order matters for performance even though all five give identical results.
claims.quote: It is apparent that methods C1 and C5 require significantly fewer floating-point operations than the other alternatives for the typical case in the QR factorization, i.e., for n1 large and k relatively small. The C1 method requires the smallest number of floating-point operations of these methods for all updates that occur in RGEQRF for a factorization of an m ⫻ n matrix if m ⱖ n. ... Therefore, the routine DQTC implements method C1. The routine DLARFB called by the LAPACK algorithm DGEQRF also implements the C1 method

claims.claim: Forming T (the cost of the I−YTY^T representation) is the dominant extra cost of blocked vs. unblocked QR and grows cubically in block size k (the T recurrence is T(m,k)=T(m,k1)+T(m−k1,k2)+k1·k2·(2m−k1)), whereas the per-step benefit of using T in the k−1 updates is negligible by comparison. Consequently pure recursion (doubling k up to n/2, cost (13/6)n^3) is far more expensive than a fixed small block size; the recommended hybrid (RGEQRF, optimal nb≈48) recurses only within a small panel and keeps the dominant cubic term marginally above LAPACK DGEQRF's (4/3)n^3 — directly motivating a fixed modest block size for the n=512 dominant shape rather than full recursion.
claims.quote: The cost of RGEQR3 on an n by n matrix is (13/6)n3 ⫹ . . . , whereas the DGEQR2 cost is (4/3)n3 ⫹ . . . . Thus, to avoid this occurring, RGEQR3 should not be used until k ⫽ n/2. ... Now compare Diff(k) to T(m, k) ⫽ FT(m, k). T(m, k) is at least four times more costly to compute ... The point we make here is that the additional cost of using T in k ⫺ 1 calls to DQTC of RGEQR3 is tiny compared to the cost of producing it. ... In our implementation we found k ⫽ 48 to be an optimal blocking factor for RGEQRF.

claims.quote: A user encountered an assertion failure when using `tl.dot()` with 3D tensors in a batched matrix multiplication kernel. ... "Assertion `idx < size()' failed" in llvm/ADT/SmallVector.h:304

claims.claim: Shifted CholeskyQR adds a positive diagonal shift to the Gram matrix, computing the Cholesky factorization of A^T A + sI instead of A^T A, which guarantees the Cholesky step does not break down on ill-conditioned matrices. This is the key fix that lets a CholeskyQR-family (triangular-orthogonalization) method be applied to inputs where naive CholeskyQR fails — directly relevant to the contract's requirement to handle ill-conditioned/near-rank-deficient inputs without squaring the condition number catastrophically.
claims.quote: we extend the applicability to κ2(X) = O(u−1) by introducing a shift to the computed Gram matrix so as to guarantee the Cholesky factorization R^T R = A^T A + sI succeeds numerically.

claims.claim: The recommended shift value is s = α‖X‖₂² with the explicit constant α = 11{mn + n(n+1)}u (u = unit roundoff, m×n the matrix size), and because ‖X‖₂ is expensive to compute it can be replaced by ‖X‖_F to give a (larger, conservative) shift. This is a concrete, implementable formula for choosing the shift in a custom kernel.
claims.quote: of breakdown we take α = 11{mn + n(n + 1)}u, so the condition number of Q̂ is ... In practice, since kXk2 is expensive to compute we can estimate it reliably using ... kXkF, which results in a larger (more conservative) shift.

claims.claim: Standard (naive) CholeskyQR forms the Gram matrix A^T A, which squares the condition number and makes the Cholesky factorization break down for ill-conditioned matrices; CholeskyQR2 (running it twice) only works up to κ2(X) ≲ u^(-1/2), whereas the shifted variant plus CholeskyQR2 (shiftedCholeskyQR3) extends the working range to κ2(X) = O(u^(-1)). This quantifies exactly why the prompt's warning that 'naive CholeskyQR squares the condition number will FAIL' is correct, and the conditioning ceiling of the family.
claims.quote: A recent work establishes that the ... κ2(X) = O(u−1/2) ... In this work we extend the applicability to κ2(X) = O(u−1) ... After the shift, CholeskyQR2 safely computes the QR factorization on AR−1.

claims.claim: shiftedCholeskyQR3 (one shifted step plus CholeskyQR2) yields a backward-stable QR factorization with orthogonality ‖Q^T Q − I‖₂ = O(u) and residual ‖A − QR‖_F/‖A‖_F = O(u), i.e. both at the unit-roundoff level. This is the accuracy guarantee that determines whether the method could pass the checker's orthogonality and factor-residual tolerances when implemented in the appropriate precision.
claims.quote: we obtain the required QR factorization with excellent orthogonality kQ^T Q − Ik = O(u) and residual kA − QRkF/kAkF = O(u), overall a backward stable QR factorization.

claims.claim: The method is rich in BLAS-3 (GEMM/SYRK) operations and is easily parallelized — it ran more than ten times faster than Gram-Schmidt and achieved up to 40x speedup over alternatives in the authors' experiments. This supports the strategic point that a CholeskyQR-type approach maps almost entirely onto tensor-core GEMMs (attractive for the B200 batched regime), trading the sequential panel dependency of Householder for matmul throughput.
claims.quote: an advantage of shiftedCholeskyQR3 is that it is rich in BLAS-3 operations and easily parallelized (it ran more than ten times faster than Gram-Schmidt ... we achieve significant (up to x40) speedup over alternative methods.

claims.claim: Block Householder QR (BQR) — the level-3 BLAS / compact-WY form that LAPACK's dgeqrf uses — is provably as backward-stable as the standard unblocked HQR despite more FLOPs, with backward error bound ‖ΔR‖_F ≤ n·γ̃_m·‖A‖_F and near-orthogonality ‖Q̂_BQR − Q‖_F ≤ n^{3/2}·γ̃_m. This validates the blocked compact-WY recurrence as the numerically sound basis for a custom kernel that produces the geqrf-packed (H,tau) form.
claims.quote: this section shows that BQR is as numerically stable as HQR despite requiring more FLOPs. In fact, many linear algebra libraries such as LAPACK use a variant of BQR as the QR factorization algorithm (see dgeqrf of [2]).

claims.claim: Mixed-precision block QR using NVIDIA TensorCore bFMAs with FP16 inputs (mpBQR3) is 3 to 4 orders of magnitude LESS accurate than its FP32 counterpart — backward error near u(fp16)≈5e-4 — even at the most favorable block size r=n (whole-matrix block). This is a direct, falsifiable warning that a naive FP16 tensor-core QR will NOT meet the contract's rtol=20·n·eps32 ≈ 2.4e-6·n FP32-level tolerance; FP32-accurate output requires emulation (e.g. 3xTF32/split-float) or refinement, not plain FP16/BF16 tensor cores.
claims.quote: the rightmost data for mpBQR3 (corresponds to r = n), is still between 3 and 4 orders of magnitude less accurate than its high precision variant.

claims.claim: In TensorCore bFMA QR the dominant error source is CASTING THE WY (V,T) REPRESENTATION DOWN to low precision before the tensor-core matrix product, NOT the bFMA accumulation itself (which uses high-precision internal accumulation and is comparatively small). Implication: keeping the GEMM accumulator in FP32 does not rescue accuracy if the V/T operands are stored in FP16/BF16 — the precision loss is in the operand cast, which is exactly what a split-float/3xTF32 emulation scheme must address.
claims.quote: since the rounding errors from the bFMAs are small in comparison to the errors from casting down the WY representation built in high precision.

claims.claim: Backward error of mixed-precision QR increases monotonically as the matrix condition number grows; the authors explicitly construct ill-conditioned test matrices (via A = castdown(Q1·D·Q2) with logarithmically spaced singular values) and observe stability is not guaranteed. This confirms that the contract's ill-conditioned / near-rank-deficient / clustered-singular-value inputs are the binding accuracy constraint that gates how aggressively low precision can be used internally.
claims.quote: The leftmost plot of Figure 3 shows the backward errors of mpHQR2 increasing as the theoretical condition numbers of the generated random matrices increase, and ... that stability is not guaranteed.

claims.claim: The row-partitioned Tall-and-Skinny QR (TSQR / AllReduce) variant can be both FASTER and MORE accurate than traditional HQR in low precision for ill-conditioned, extremely overdetermined cases — even when the derived error bounds suggest the opposite — making it more robust against reduced precision. Relevant to designing the panel (tall-skinny column-block) factorization of a custom blocked QR kernel for the large-batch regime.
claims.quote: our numerical simulations (discussed in section 5) show that TSQR can not only increase the speed but also achieve higher accuracy than the traditional HQR factorization in low precisions.
