results.title: CuTe DSL Blackwell SM100 persistent batched D = alpha*A*B + beta*C GEMM (Python)
results.snippet: THE single most relevant DSL example for the QR trailing update. It is a persistent, warp-specialized, batched (L = batch dim) Blackwell SM100 GEMM that computes D = alpha*A*B + beta*C in pure Python CuTe DSL. The Householder trailing update A := A - V*(T^T*(V^T*A)) is exactly this alpha/beta form (alpha=-1, beta=1), so you get the rank-update fused without a separate AXPY pass. Docstring spells out the full Blackwell pipeline: DMA warp loads A/B GMEM->SMEM via TMA; MMA warp issues tcgen05.mma writing the accumulator to TMEM; EPILOGUE warp does tcgen05.ld TMEM->RMEM, loads C, computes D = alpha*acc + beta*C, type-converts, and TMA-stores. Crucially it exposes an `epilogue_op` lambda hook (e.g. relu via cute.where) -- you can fuse an elementwise step into the trailing update. Run flags: --ab_dtype Float16/BFloat16, --acc_dtype Float32, --mma_tiler_mn 256,128, --cluster_shape_mn 2,1, --use_2cta_instrs, --alpha/--beta. Note: NOTE the path moved to .../cute/blackwell/kernel/dense_gemm/ in current main.

results.title: CuTe DSL Blackwell SM100 grouped GEMM with distinct per-group problem sizes (Python)
results.snippet: The closest DSL analog to a batched QR with mixed n (32/176/352/512/1024/2048/4096). Implements grouped GEMM (distinct M,N,K per group) as a TMA + tcgen05 warp-specialized PERSISTENT kernel; per-group pointers, shapes, and strides live in GMEM arrays and a tile scheduler walks all groups across a persistent grid (--tensormap_update_mode SMEM/GMEM). Directly informs whether to issue one persistent megakernel over all batch matrices vs. a sequence of batched-GEMM calls (deliverable 4/6): grouped-GEMM's GMEM problem-shape array is the mechanism for fanning hundreds of independent small/medium trailing updates into one launch. Constraints relevant to FP32 QR output: inputs MUST be fp16/bf16 (so FP32 panels need a TF32/split path), output can be fp16/bf16/FP32, l (batch) per group must be 1, majorness must match across groups, tcgen05 MMA tile e.g. (128,64). Example problem_sizes include (640,...) and (16,...) groups -- the same small/large mix as the scored shapes.

results.title: Colfax: Writing GEMM Kernels Using Tensor Memory (TMEM) for Blackwell GPUs
results.snippet: The canonical narrative reference for the tcgen05/TMEM mechanics every approach here depends on, with code. Establishes: UMMA = tcgen05.mma (replaces WGMMA), D=A*B(+D), ONLY ONE THREAD launches the MMA; operand A in TMEM-or-SMEM, B in SMEM only, accumulator in TMEM only (eliminates register pressure but you must copy it out). TMEM = 256KB/SM = 512 cols x 128 lanes of 32-bit cells; allocation granularity power-of-2, min 32 cols, alloc/dealloc from same warp (`TMEM::Allocator1Sm`). Accumulator copied to registers via `tcgen05.ld` / `SM100_TMEM_LOAD_*` atoms with `make_tmem_copy`; each warp only sees 32 of 128 TMEM lanes (warpgroup epilogue). Supported MMA kinds: .kind::f16 (FP16/BF16), .kind::tf32, .kind::f8f6f4 with block scaling -- confirms the TF32 tensor-core path for FP32-input QR. A/B use 64-bit SMEM descriptors, K-major + swizzle (UMMA::Layout_K_SW128_Atom). Read this to understand why the trailing update naturally lands its accumulator in TMEM and how to drain it before the next panel.

results.title: CuTe DSL Blackwell SM100 dense GEMM reference (Python) — TF32 path + tcgen05 atom construction
results.snippet: The base DSL GEMM that shows, in concrete Python, how to stand up a tcgen05 kernel and -- key for FP32 QR -- the automatic FP32->TF32 tensor-core path. The MMA atom is built with `sm100_utils.make_trivial_tiled_mma(ab_dtype, ..., acc_dtype, tcgen05.CtaGroup.ONE/TWO)`; when an operand element_type is `cutlass.Float32` the example passes `cutlass.TFloat32` to the MMA (lines ~390/407), i.e. FP32 inputs are consumed as TF32 by the tensor core while `acc_dtype=cutlass.Float32`. Documents the hard tcgen05 tile constraints you must respect when tiling 512x512 / 1024 / 2048: MMA tiler M must be 64 or 128 (128/256 with use_2cta_instrs), N must be 32..256 in steps of 32; A/B counts multiples of 4/8/16 for TF32 / FP16-BF16 / Int8-FP8. SMEM layouts via make_smem_layout_a/b/epi; TMEM columns sized by _compute_num_tmem_alloc_cols. Import surface: `from cutlass.cute.nvgpu import cpasync, tcgen05` + `cutlass.utils.blackwell_helpers as sm100_utils`.

results.title: CuTe DSL Blackwell EFC: custom fused epilogue GEMM (Y=A*B and D=alpha*A*B+beta*C+x_factor*X)
results.snippet: The mechanism for FUSING panel work into the trailing update (deliverable 3's 'fuse panel+update'). Uses Epilogue Fusion Configuration (EFC) to emit, from one tcgen05 GEMM, BOTH the raw accumulator Y=A*B and a multi-input affine combination D = alpha*A*B + beta*C + x_factor*X -- multiple read-only inputs (C, X) and multiple outputs (D, Y) in a single epilogue. For QR this shows how to compute and store the trailing update while simultaneously emitting an auxiliary tensor (e.g. a partial W = T^T*(V^T*A) factor or a residual) in the same pass, avoiding extra GMEM round-trips. Companion files in the same efc/ dir: common_dense_gemm_efc.py (DenseGemmEFC base), activation_custom_epilogue_dense_gemm.py, synthetic_custom_epilogue_dense_gemm.py. Subclass DenseGemmEFC and override the epilogue. Medium (not high) only because the affine recipe is illustrative, not a QR primitive out of the box.

results.title: CUTLASS CuTe DSL Blackwell GEMM tutorial series (fp16_gemm_0..6, nvfp4_gemm_0..1)
results.snippet: The graduated learning path to get from zero to a working tcgen05 DSL kernel before attempting QR-specific fusion. A staged sequence (fp16_gemm_0.py basic TMA+SMEM+Tensor Core through _6, plus nvfp4_gemm_0/1 and utils.py) that incrementally adds: multi-stage software pipelining via `cutlass.range(..., prefetch_stages=...)`, epilogue tiling to avoid bursty writeback and cut register pressure, and warp/block-level parallelism. Most useful for deliverable 3 as the on-ramp: it isolates each Blackwell GEMM optimization (pipeline, epilogue tiling) in its own file so you can lift exactly the pieces the QR trailing-update kernel needs. Lower relevance than the dense/grouped/EFC examples because it is FP16-only pedagogy with no batching or alpha/beta, but it is the recommended starting point for anyone new to the DSL.

claims.claim: For batched factorization of tiny matrices (size up to 32), the optimal design is one-kernel/one-CUDA-threadblock-per-matrix with fully unblocked computation and read/write-each-matrix-exactly-once, because the computation is memory-bound at these sizes and the entire matrix stays cached in fast memory (registers or shared memory) for the whole factorization, making LAPACK-style panel blocking pointless.
claims.quote: First, each matrix is factorized using exactly one CUDA thread block (TB). Upon launch, the kernel is configured with as many TBs as the number of matrices... Second, we adopt an optimal memory traffic strategy. Each matrix will be read and written exactly once... Finally, all kernels use unblocked computations. There is no need to factorize a panel of width nb > 1 so that the trailing updates use L3 BLAS operations that are rich in data reuse... each matrix is entirely kept in registers or shared memory, which means that data reuse is preserved anyway.

claims.claim: A 1D thread configuration (N threads per matrix) decisively outperforms a 2D (N×N threads) configuration for batched tiny-matrix factorization, because the 2D layout (e.g. 256 threads for a 16×16 matrix) caps resident threadblocks per SM and kills occupancy; measured speedups are 10.5×/9.6× (single/double) for Cholesky and ~9× or more for LU and QR on a Pascal P100.
claims.quote: Fig. 1 shows speedups of 10.5×/9.6× in single/double precision against the 2D configuration for the Cholesky factorization. A similar 9× (or more) speedup is obtained for the LU factorization in both precisions (Fig. 2). Fig. 3 also shows similar significant speedups for the QR factorization. It is clear that, regardless of the numerical algorithm, the 1D configuration is the winning strategy for batch workloads of small sizes.

claims.claim: QR factorization uniquely favors shared-memory (or a hybrid: registers for storage + shared memory for communication) over a pure-register/warp-shuffle implementation — the opposite of LU and Cholesky — because the inner y = vᵀC matvec in the Householder update needs Q×log2(Np2) reduction steps with shuffles (rounding N up to a power of two) versus only P steps with shared memory where each y element maps to one thread.
claims.quote: Unlike the Cholesky and LU factorizations, we observe that the shared memory version is faster than the register version, which is the opposite of our initial expectations... the total number of reduction steps is Q×log2 (Np2 ), and not Q×log2 (P)... If both v and C are in shared memory, we can assign each element of y to a single thread... using Q threads, it would take only P steps to find the entire vector y... Fig. 8 shows that the register version with shared memory communication beats the pure shared memory implementation.

claims.claim: Packing multiple matrices into one threadblock (concurrency control, tuning parameter nFTB, swept 1–16) only improves performance for matrix sizes 1 through 16 and gives no gain for sizes larger than 16, because above 16 the hardware already rounds the thread count up to a full warp; QR gains in this small range were 2.0×–3.8× (single) and 1.8×–3.8× (double).
claims.quote: We observe that a tunable nFTB does not affect the performance for sizes larger than 16. For such range, the hardware rounds up the number of threads to use a full warp anyway... For sizes 1 through 16, we observe performance gains in both single and double precision. The smaller the sizes, the more the speedups... the QR factorization performance is enhanced by factors that range from 2.0× to 3.8× in single precision, and from 1.8× to 3.8× in double precision.

claims.claim: The entire approach is explicitly scoped to tiny matrices of size 1 to 32 (one million of them) on Pascal P100 and Volta V100 GPUs; final batched QR reached up to 11.8× over cuBLAS in single precision on V100 (2.1×–11.04× on P100) but exhibited double-precision performance stagnation attributed to the N×N shared-memory requirement limiting SM occupancy.
claims.quote: we present GPU design and optimization techniques for high-performance batched one-sided factorizations of millions of tiny matrices (of size 32 and less)... Considering the results on the V100 GPU (Fig. 20), MAGMA is up to 11.8× faster than cuBLAS in single precision... We observe a kind of stagnation in the double precision performance for MAGMA... The shared memory requirements for this kernel (N×N) seem to limit the multiprocessor occupancy.

claims.claim: Triton (unlike CUDA) provides no programmer access to GPU registers, so a kernel cannot implement a custom register-caching strategy and must instead rely on Triton's compiler to manage shared-memory/register placement. This is a concrete expressibility limit for hand-written QR panel kernels that want reflector vectors / T-matrix tiles pinned in registers.
claims.quote: In contrast to CUDA, Triton gives no access to registers on the GPU. Therefore, we cannot apply the custom caching strategy of the fused CUDA kernels and instead rely on Triton for managing the shared memory and register cache.

claims.claim: Triton has no grid-level synchronization between programs and cannot communicate values between programs via HBM; in the one-program-per-matrix (per-head) design this caps the per-program working dimension (head dimension limited to 128 forward / 64 backward on H100). A single-threadblock unblocked Householder QR in Triton is therefore size-bounded by what fits without cross-program sync, and large n (e.g. 512/1024) cannot be handled by one cooperating program-group in Triton the way a CUDA cooperative grid can.
claims.quote: Additionally, there is no (grid) synchronization between programs in Triton, which makes it impossible to communicate values between different programs over HBM. In section 6.1 we find that this poses a limitation on the maximum head dimension of 128 for the forward pass and 64 for the backward pass on a NVIDIA H100 GPU.

claims.claim: On an H100/Hopper-class SM the register file is 256 KB and shared memory is up to 228 KB per SM/block; a 768x768 weight matrix (~4 MB) therefore cannot fit on one SM and must be sharded across multiple SMs in a cooperative grid group that synchronizes at grid level. This directly bounds the largest n a one-matrix-per-threadblock QR can keep resident: a 512x512 FP32 panel/matrix is 1 MB, far exceeding 228 KB SRAM, so only column-panel tiles (not the full matrix) fit in shared memory, forcing a blocked/cooperative-grid approach for large n.
claims.quote: For a large hidden or head dimension d, e.g. d = 768, the recurrent weight matrix for an LSTM has the size 4 × 768 × 768 × 2 B ≈ 4 MB. However, for an H100 GPU, the register file size is 256KB and the SRAM / shared memory is up to 228KB per SM / block. Therefore, this matrix needs to be sharded over multiple SMs in a cooperative grid group that can synchronize on the grid level.

claims.claim: Triton's tl.dot tensor-core matrix-multiply has a minimum block size of 16x16, which imposes a minimum batch/tile size; smaller dimensions must be zero-padded at an efficiency cost. For the small-n large-batch QR shape (n=32, and panel widths in blocked QR which are typically small, e.g. 16-64), this means Triton tensor-core GEMMs for the trailing update or panel may be forced to pad up to 16x16 tiles, wasting work.
claims.quote: The recurrent matrix multiply in equation 1 and 3 is implemented with Triton’s matrix multiply operation tl.dot which gives an interface to the Tensor Core units on GPUs. In Triton minimum block size of these matrix multiplies is 16x16, which gives a limit on the minimum batch size. In practice, we enable smaller batch sizes by padding zeros at the cost of efficiency.

claims.claim: For the small-head (small-n analog) regime, the Triton fused kernel is about 2x faster than the CUDA fused kernel at head dimensions 16 and 32, whereas CUDA's register-resident persistent kernel wins and scales to much larger sizes (up to 768+). This supports a regime-split strategy: Triton one-program-per-matrix is competitive for tiny matrices (n=32), but a CUDA persistent/cooperative-grid kernel is preferable for the dominant large-n shapes (512/1024).
claims.quote: The Triton kernels are limited to head dimension 128 and 64, but are about two times faster than CUDA fused for small head dimensions 16 and 32. The fused CUDA kernels support all head dimensions up to 768 (actually more, see Appendix Section H.1) and are about two to three times faster than the alternating kernels.

claims.claim: No single design strategy serves all batch QR sizes efficiently; the optimal kernel structure must be selected by matrix size, and following the standard LAPACK QR building-block structure is significantly outperformed by non-standard fused kernels that increase data reuse. This directly validates the research plan to pursue distinct approaches for the n=32, n=176/352, and n=512 regimes rather than one kernel.
claims.quote: We show that there is not a single design strategy that can serve all sizes eﬃciently. Each design strategy assumes a number of building blocks (e.g., GPU kernels) of the factorization, which might diﬀer from the conventional LAPACK structure... following the LAPACK QR design convention, while still useful, is signiﬁcantly outperformed by unconventional code structures that increase data reuse.

claims.claim: For tiny matrices (square sizes up to 32), a fully fused, fully unrolled unblocked dgeqr2 kept in registers/shared memory is fastest; it uses SERIAL reduction (faster than parallel reduction with repeated syncs at sub-warp dimensions), packs multiple matrices per warp (e.g. one warp factorizes four 8x8 matrices), and is template-instantiated per (m,n). This yields up to 3.22x speedup over the best competition. Directly maps to the batch=20,n=32 scored shape.
claims.quote: A ﬁnal optimization is possible when the entire matrix can be cached in the register ﬁle or in the shared memory. At this point, a fully fused and unrolled dgeqr2 is used... First, it uses a serial reduction for computing the norm of a column, and for the v T × A product. For sub-warp dimensions, we found out that a serial reduction is often faster than a parallel reduction with repetitive synchronizations. Second, one warp can be involved in factorizing more than one matrix simultaneously. For example, a single warp can factorize four 8 × 8 matrices at the same time... the Figure shows signiﬁcant speedups, up to 3.22× against the best competition.

claims.claim: The register-file panel kernel assigns one thread per matrix row, so a 512-row panel needs 512 threads, capping the SM at 4 thread blocks (hardware limit); panels taller than 512 rows incur at least a 25% occupancy drop. The remedy is a second kernel that stores the panel in shared memory with a tunable thread count (nb <= threads <= m), with offline tuning choosing register-vs-shared and the thread count. Critical occupancy guidance for the dominant batch=640,n=512 case.
claims.quote: The performance of this kernel is dependent on the height of the panel, since it requires one thread per row. For example, a panel of size 512 × nb needs 512 threads. Assuming that all other resources are not a bottleneck, we can schedule four thread blocks at maximum per SM, due to a hardware limitation. Panels taller than 512 would cause at least 25% drop in the thread occupancy per SM... We propose a second kernel that stores the panel in shared memory instead. This enables us use any number of threads to factorize the panel. The proposed kernel assumes nb ≤#threads≤ m.

claims.claim: Fused panel + fused trailing-update kernels can factorize an ENTIRE matrix without any batch GEMM call, applying elementary reflectors directly to the trailing matrix in shared memory/registers WITHOUT forming the T factor; this beats the LAPACK-style batch-GEMM path below a tuned cutoff width determined by offline sweeps and stored in lookup tables. Strong evidence that a persistent megakernel can beat a sequence of batched-GEMM calls for medium n.
claims.quote: An important point is that the fused panel and update kernels can be used to factorize the entire matrix, without utilizing the batch dgemm kernel... since the fused kernels operate on the fastest memory levels of the GPU, the implementation can be simpliﬁed into applying the elementary reﬂectors directly to the trailing matrix (without forming the T factor)... we conducted a set of oﬄine tuning sweeps that discover the cut-oﬀ width, below which we should use the fused panel/update kernels. The results from the tuning sweeps are stored in lookup tables.

claims.claim: The compact-WY block reflector Q = I - V*T*V^T enables a GEMM-based trailing update, but forming the T factor (dlarft) is costly for thin panels: the improved algorithm aggregates all the dgemv calls into a single dgemm (T = V^T*V then a per-column triangular product), yet requires preprocessing (copy R to workspace, zero V's upper triangle and set unit diagonal, copy R back) whose auxiliary kernels (dlacpy/dlaset) can dominate runtime for thin panels (e.g. 45% of time at 128x16). Directly informs items 1 and 4 on whether to form T at all.
claims.quote: the factor Tnb×nb can be computed recursively as in Algorithm 1... However, previous work [11] has shown that all the calls to dgemv can be aggregated into one dgemm call, while the dtrmv calls remain roughly unchanged... In order to call dgemm, the matrix V must be separated from the R factor... This requires (1) copying the R matrix into a workspace (dlacpy), (2) setting the upper triangular part of V to zeros, with units on the diagonal (dlaset), and (3) another copy to bring R back on top of V (dlacpy).

claims.claim: CUTLASS ships an official CuTe DSL Python example for Blackwell SM100 that computes a batched D = alpha*A*B + beta*C GEMM, demonstrating exactly the trailing-update form (A := A - V*T*Vᵀ*A maps to a GEMM with alpha=-1, beta=1) needed for blocked Householder QR; the class is SM100PersistentDenseGemmAlphaBetaKernel.
claims.quote:
class SM100PersistentDenseGemmAlphaBetaKernel:
    """Batched matrix multiplication (D = alpha * A * B + beta * C) with support for various data types and architectural features specific to Blackwell GPUs with persistent tile scheduling and warp specialization."""

claims.claim: The Blackwell tensor-core GEMM in CuTe DSL uses tcgen05 instructions selected via tcgen05.CtaGroup (ONE or TWO for 2-CTA cooperative MMA), with MMA reading operands from shared memory and writing accumulators to Tensor Memory (TMEM) — this is the concrete sm_100 5th-gen tensor-core programming model for the QR trailing update.

The kernel supports TFloat32, Float16, and BFloat16 (plus FP8/INT8) input types for A/B with Float32 accumulation, confirming the TF32/BF16-input-with-FP32-accumulate path on Blackwell tensor cores that a mixed-precision QR trailing update would use while keeping FP32 accuracy.
claims.quote: Input A/B types (must match): TFloat32, Float16, BFloat16, Int8, Uint8, Float8E4M3FN, Float8E5M2 ... Accumulator types: Float32 (all floating-point A/B)

claims.claim: The example uses native batching via an L (batch) dimension on all tensors (A: MxKxL, B: NxKxL, C/D: MxNxL) combined with a StaticPersistentTileScheduler, providing a directly reusable template for the large-batch QR regime (e.g. batch=640) where many independent matrices are processed by one persistent kernel rather than separate launches.
claims.quote: Input tensor shapes: A: MxKxL (L = batch dimension), B: NxKxL, C, D: MxNxL ... tile_sched = utils.StaticPersistentTileScheduler.create(...) work_tile = tile_sched.initial_work_tile_info() while work_tile.is_valid_tile: ... tile_sched.advance_to_next_work()

claims.claim: The CuTe DSL kernel achieves performance via warp specialization with distinct roles — TMA-load warp (GMEM→SMEM), MMA warp issuing tcgen05.mma, and epilogue warps doing TMEM→RMEM and the alpha/beta scale — coordinated by named barriers and multiple producer-consumer pipelines (AB, accumulator, C), which is the structural pattern a hand-written Blackwell QR trailing-update fusion must replicate.
claims.quote:
self.epilog_warp_ids = (0, 1, 2, 3)  # Epilogue computation
self.mma_warp_id = 4                  # Matrix multiply-accumulate
self.tma_warp_id = 5                  # Tensor Memory Access (DMA) ... Named barriers coordinate cross-warp synchronization.

claims.claim: NVIDIA ships a Blackwell SM100 grouped-GEMM example written in pure Python CuTe DSL, using @cute.jit for host orchestration and @cute.kernel for the device kernel, in a class GroupedGemmKernel — demonstrating that batched/grouped GEMM (variable per-group M/N/K) is expressible in the CuTe DSL on B200.
claims.quote: Yes, this is pure Python CuTe DSL. Key decorators: @cute.jit def __call__(self, ...): # Host-side orchestration; @cute.kernel def kernel(self, ...): # GPU device kernel. The class GroupedGemmKernel wraps configuration, tensormap management, and kernel launch.

claims.claim: The grouped GEMM uses Blackwell 5th-gen tcgen05 tensor-core MMA atoms with selectable 1-CTA or 2-CTA group instructions (tcgen05.CtaGroup.ONE / TWO), and uses TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) for A/B/C transfers — the exact tcgen05 path a trailing-update QR GEMM would target on sm_100.
claims.quote: The kernel uses Blackwell's tcgen05 MMA architecture with configurable CTA groups: self.cta_group = (tcgen05.CtaGroup.TWO if use_2cta_instrs else tcgen05.CtaGroup.ONE)

claims.claim: This grouped-GEMM kernel only accepts FP16 and BF16 inputs (no native FP32/TF32 input path), though the accumulator dtype is independently parameterized (e.g. FP32 accumulation) and outputs may be fp16/bf16/fp32 — so an FP32 QR trailing update cannot use this example as-is without a split-float/precision strategy.
claims.quote: "Only fp16 and bf16 data types are supported as inputs. Output data types could be fp16, bf16 or fp32." ... Accumulator dtype is parameterized independently (acc_dtype), enabling FP16->FP32 accumulation.

claims.claim: Grouped GEMM handles distinct per-group problem sizes via device-side tensors (problem_shape_mnkl, strides_abc, tensor_address_abc) plus a StaticPersistentGroupTileScheduler that dynamically assigns tiles to CTAs and updates TMA tensormap descriptors when switching groups — the mechanism for batching hundreds of independent matrices of differing sizes in one launch.
claims.quote: A persistent tile scheduler (StaticPersistentGroupTileScheduler) dynamically assigns work tiles to CTAs, querying problem dimensions at runtime ... The TMA warp updates tensormap descriptors when switching groups to reflect new tensor geometry.

claims.claim: The kernel is a single persistent megakernel: one CTA is launched per SM and a tile scheduler load-balances groups across CTAs (a CTA can process multiple groups), using warp-specialized async pipelines (PipelineTmaUmma for TMA loads, PipelineUmmaAsync for accumulator stages) and named barriers — evidence that a persistent-kernel design outperforms a sequence of separate batched launches for many small/medium matrices.
claims.quote: The design uses a persistent kernel where one CTA per SM launches initially ... "When the problem shapes are on device, we launch one CTA per SM. The if condition later prevents the warps from extra CTAs from doing any work." ... ab_pipeline = pipeline.PipelineTmaUmma.create(...) # TMA loads; acc_pipeline = pipeline.PipelineUmmaAsync.create(...) # Accumulator stages

claims.claim: Blackwell sm_100 5th-gen tensor cores use the tcgen05.mma PTX instruction (called UMMA in CUTLASS), which computes asynchronous D = A*B + D and replaces Hopper's WGMMA; only one warp launches the UMMAs and synchronization uses mbarriers (umma_arrive). This is the instruction a hand-written trailing-update GEMM (A := (I − VTVᵀ)A) must target on B200.
claims.quote: Blackwell introduced the `tcgen05.mma` instruction for MMA. In CUTLASS, `tcgen05.mma` is referred to as UMMA. ... Just like WGMMA for Hopper, UMMA is asynchronous and hence requires synchronization... Only one warp launches the UMMAs.

claims.claim: Tensor Memory (TMEM) on Blackwell is 256KB per SM, organized as 512 columns x 128 rows (lanes) of 32-bit cells, allocated via tcgen05.alloc (column count must be a power of 2, >=32) and freed via tcgen05.dealloc; this is a distinct memory space from the 228KB shared-memory budget and is where all UMMA accumulators must live.
claims.quote: TMEM is 256KB per SM in size, and is organized 2-dimensionally in 512 columns and 128 rows, or lanes, of 32-bit cells. ... TMEM is allocated dynamically using the `tcgen05.alloc` instruction... The number of columns allocated must be a power of 2 and at least 32... TMEM must be explicitly deallocated with `tcgen05.dealloc`.

claims.claim: For tcgen05/UMMA, the accumulator must be in TMEM, the second input (B) must be in SMEM, and the first input (A) may come from either SMEM or TMEM; results are copied out of TMEM to registers with the tcgen05.ld instruction (e.g. via the SM100_TMEM_LOAD_32dp32b1x TiledCopy). This constrains data-flow design for a custom QR trailing-update GEMM.
claims.quote: UMMA can either accept the first input from SMEM or TMEM, the second input must be in SMEM, and the accumulator must be in TMEM. ... Once all the MMAs are done, we need to copy the accumulator results from TMEM to registers. This is done using the PTX `tcgen05.ld` instruction.

claims.claim: tcgen05/UMMA supports FP16/BF16 inputs with FP32 accumulation via the CUTLASS atom SM100_MMA_F16BF16_SS (SS = both operands in SMEM; TS variant sources A from TMEM), giving a concrete tensor-core path for the BF16/FP16-internal mixed-precision QR strategy on Blackwell.
claims.quote: SM100_MMA_F16BF16_SS<TypeA, TypeB, TypeC, 128, 256, UMMA::Major::K, UMMA::Major::K> ... SS indicates both A and B sourced from SMEM ... TS variant sources A from TMEM and B from SMEM

claims.claim: tcgen05/UMMA supported matrix tile shapes are 64 x N x 16 (N a multiple of 8) and 128 x N x 16 (N a multiple of 16), with N at most 256 — meaning the trailing-update GEMM must be tiled into M-of-64/128, K-of-16 blocks with N<=256 to map onto a single UMMA instruction.
claims.quote: 64 x N x 16 with N a multiple of 8 and 128 x N x 16 with N a multiple of 16, where N is at most 256.

claims.claim: The CuTe DSL Blackwell SM100 GEMM constructs the tcgen05 MMA atom in Python via sm100_utils.make_trivial_tiled_mma(a_dtype, a_major_mode, b_major_mode, acc_dtype, cta_group, mma_tiler[:2]), giving a high-level Python API to build 5th-gen tensor-core MMAs without writing PTX — directly usable for the QR trailing-update GEMM.
claims.quote:
tiled_mma = sm100_utils.make_trivial_tiled_mma(
    self.a_dtype,
    self.a_major_mode,
    self.b_major_mode,
    self.acc_dtype,
    self.cta_group,
    self.mma_tiler[:2],
)

claims.claim: TFloat32 (TF32) and Float16/BFloat16 are supported A/B input dtypes for the Blackwell tcgen05 GEMM, and Float32 is a valid accumulator type for ALL floating-point A/B dtypes — so a TF32-input/FP32-accumulate GEMM (and BF16-input/FP32-accumulate) is natively expressible, which is exactly the mixed-precision path needed to keep an FP32-accurate trailing update A := (I − VTVᵀ)A.
claims.quote:
:note: Supported A/B data types:
    - TFloat32

result.evidence: The claim bundles 3 assertions; the load-bearing one overreaches. (1) HARDWARE FACTS hold: NVIDIA Hopper Tuning Guide confirms H100 RF=256KB/SM and SRAM up to 228KB/SM; 512x512 FP32 = exactly 1,048,576 B = 1MB > 228KB. (2) "Only column-panel tiles, not the full matrix, fit in SRAM" is CORRECT and confirmed by the MAGMA batch-QR SOTA (Abdelfattah/Tomov/Dongarra, ICCS 2022, iccs-meeting.org/.../133500064.pdf): the kernel "caches a panel of size m x nb in the register file," the trailing matrix stays in global memory and is streamed in blocks ("read the next block of columns from the trailing panel"). (3) "FORCING a ... COOPERATIVE-GRID approach for large n" / "sharded across multiple SMs in a cooperative grid group" is an OVERREACH imported from a DIFFERENT algorithm. The source (arXiv 2412.07752) is FlashRNN (I/O-aware RNN/LSTM optimization), NOT QR; its cooperative-grid sharding applies to a SINGLE large LSTM recurrent weight matrix REUSED at every timestep of a sequential recurrence, so it must stay grid-resident. For BATCHED independent QR at n=512 the SOTA assigns ONE THREAD BLOCK PER MATRIX with NO grid-level cooperative sync: a 512-row panel maps to a single block (512 threads, one per row), and "panels taller than 512 cause a 25% occupancy drop" — i.e., 512 is precisely the size a single block still serves. "Blocked" (panel-in-SRAM + GEMM trailing update, one block/matrix) is NOT "cooperative-grid sharding of one matrix across SMs"; the claim conflates them. The dominant scored workload (batch=640, n=512) is therefore the canonical one-block-per-matrix regime, directly contradicting "forcing ... cooperative-grid." MISATTRIBUTION: the source's "~4MB" = 4 gate matrices x 768x768 x 2B (BF16); the claim restates it as "a 768x768 weight matrix (~4MB)" — a single 768x768 matrix is 2.36MB (FP32)/1.18MB (BF16). Refuted on source-mismatch + contradicted mechanism for the strong claim, despite the SRAM-residency part being correct.

VERIFIED TRUE: (1) The quote is exact — FlashRNN paper (arxiv 2412.07752 v3, Pöppel/Beck/Hochreiter, JKU/NXAI; PDF text lines 1541–1545) says verbatim "register file size is 256KB and the SRAM / shared memory is up to 228KB per SM / block. Therefore, this matrix needs to be sharded over multiple SMs in a cooperative grid group that can synchronize on the grid level." (2) Numbers check out vs NVIDIA Hopper & Blackwell Tuning Guides: 64K×32-bit registers/SM = 256 KB; shared memory 228 KB/SM, 227 KB/block — identical on H100 (cc 9.0) AND B200 (cc 10.0). (3) Arithmetic is exact: 512×512×4B = 1,048,576 B = 1.00 MB >> 228 KB; largest full square FP32 matrix fitting in 228 KB is n≈241. So "only column-panel tiles fit, forcing a BLOCKED approach for large n" is correct and confirmed by MAGMA/Dongarra batched-QR literature.
THE OVERREACH (refutation): the conclusion says large n forces a "blocked/COOPERATIVE-GRID approach," welding cooperative-grid grid-sync onto blocked as if equivalent and as if the quote supported it for QR. It does not. The quote justifies grid-level sync ONLY for FlashRNN's single ~4 MB recurrent weight matrix processed by the whole device per timestep. For the research question's batched regime (batch=640 independent n=512 matrices), the established/optimal design is the OPPOSITE: one matrix per thread block, matrix in GLOBAL memory, panels streamed through shared memory, trailing update as GEMM, with NO cooperative-grid synchronization — cross-SM parallelism comes from the batch dimension. Dongarra et al. "Batch QR Factorization on GPUs" (netlib 2022) states each matrix "remains within a single thread block—no cooperative grid-level synchronization across multiple SMs is required"; ICL/MAGMA batched-factorization work confirms "each matrix is factorized using exactly one CUDA thread block ... as many TBs as the number of matrices," and that batched routines (one-block-per-matrix) are specifically the right tool for n≤512. Thus the cooperative-grid half of the conclusion is unsupported by the quote (for QR) and contradicted by primary sources; cooperative-grid grid-sync would actually be a poor choice for the large-batch regime since it serializes the grid on one matrix. "Blocked" ≠ "cooperative-grid."

result.summary: A hand-written batched Householder QR on B200 should use the blocked compact-WY (UT) algorithm, which natively emits exactly the (H, tau) packed form torch.geqrf returns: on exit the on/above-diagonal entries of A hold R and the sub-diagonal entries hold the reflector vectors V (implicit unit diagonal), with tau the per-reflector scalars — and the product of k reflectors aggregates as I − U T⁻¹ Uᴴ (equivalently I − VTVᵀ), turning the trailing update A := (I − VTVᵀ)A into level-3 GEMMs that map onto Blackwell tensor cores. The workload splits sharply by regime: for the tiny/per-warp shapes (n=32, and within-tile work) a one-threadblock-per-matrix unblocked kernel is right, and uniquely for QR (unlike LU/Cholesky) a shared-memory or hybrid register-storage + shared-memory-communication layout beats pure warp-shuffle, because the y = vᵀC matvec costs Q·log₂(N_p2) shuffle-reduction steps versus only P steps when v and C live in shared memory. For the dominant batch=640/n=512 regime the matrix (1 MB FP32) far exceeds the ~228 KB SRAM budget, so it must be genuinely blocked (panel factorization + T-build + trailing GEMM) rather than kept resident; a persistent Triton megakernel sized to min(NUM_SMS, total_tiles) with each program looping over multiple independent matrices is the attested structural pattern for batching these, though Triton's lack of grid-level sync and register control bounds how much of a large-n factorization one cooperating program-group can own. The verified evidence is strongest on the algebra and packing (multiple primary LAPACK/FLAME sources, unanimous) and on the small-matrix design tradeoff (peer-reviewed MAGMA/ICL primary); it is thinner and partly contested on the precise SRAM/large-n cooperative-grid bounds and on FP32-accuracy-via-tensor-core (3xTF32/mixed-precision refinement) claims, which did not survive verification and remain open.

findings.claim: The blocked compact-WY/UT algorithm aggregates k Householder reflectors as H_0 H_1 ... H_{k-1} = I − U T⁻¹ Uᴴ (equivalently the LAPACK compact-WY form I − VTVᵀ with T upper triangular), and this is the exact algebraic basis for expressing the trailing update as matrix-matrix products and for the packed (H,tau) layout torch.geqrf returns.
findings.evidence: The FLAME/LAFF source (van de Geijn, UT Austin) states verbatim 'If H_0,...,H_{k-1} are Householder transformations, then H_0 H_1 ... H_{k-1} = I − U T⁻¹ Uᴴ', defining U as the Householder vectors (unit diagonal) and T as upper triangular. This is the foundational Schreiber & Van Loan (1989) compact-WY representation (Q = I + YTYᵀ, T upper triangular) that still underpins LAPACK GEQRF; the FLAME UT form and LAPACK I−VTVᵀ differ only in whether T's diagonal stores 1/tau-scaled values or tau directly. torch.geqrf wraps LAPACK GEQRF, which 'uses a compact WY transform,' stores reflector vectors below the diagonal (=V/U) with tau separate. The trailing update A:=(I−VTVᵀ)A is the level-3 GEMM form (DLARFT builds T, DLARFB applies it).
findings.confidence_note: Two primary sources (FLAME/LAFF + the 1989 SIAM compact-WY paper), unanimous verification, timeless classical NLA result.

findings.claim: The recursive panel factorization natively produces the torch.geqrf packed form: on exit the elements on and above the diagonal of A hold the n×n upper-triangular R, and the elements below the diagonal hold the reflector vectors V with the unit diagonal not stored — exactly the (H) packing the problem contract requires (square inputs, m=n).
findings.evidence: netlib geqrt3 states verbatim 'the elements on and above the diagonal contain the N-by-N upper triangular matrix R; the elements below the diagonal are the columns of V,' with Further Details adding 'The 1's along the diagonal of V are not stored in A.' This matches LAPACK DGEQRF man pages and the PyTorch torch.geqrf docs ('elements of R are stored on and above the diagonal. Elementary reflectors ... stored below the diagonal'), which feed torch.linalg.householder_product — exactly the checker's Q reconstruction. The contract's inputs are square (batch×n×n), so geqrt3's 'N-by-N upper triangular R' is precisely the contract case; the trapezoidal caveat for m≠n is irrelevant. Note: geqrt3 itself returns the compact-WY T factor, not per-reflector tau scalars, so a kernel must also emit tau separately to match geqrf's (H,tau) output.
findings.confidence_note: Primary LAPACK reference, independently corroborated by PyTorch docs; decades-stable storage convention.

findings.claim: The composite T factor for two stacked sub-panels is T = [[T1, T3],[0, T2]] with the off-diagonal coupling block T3 = −T1·(Y1ᴴ·Y2)·T2. This is the exact GEMM-friendly recurrence for assembling the T matrix recursively from two sub-panels (the level-3 alternative to LAPACK DLARFT's level-2 bordering).
findings.evidence: The canonical LAPACK reference implementation dgeqrt3.f (Elmroth-Gustavson recursive QR) contains verbatim at line 223 'Compute T3 = T(1:N1,J1:N) = -T1 Y1^H Y2 T2' and at lines 243-244 the block structure 'T = [T1 T3] / [ 0 T2]', with T1/Y1 from the first panel (line 186 'Q1 = I - Y1 T1 Y1^H') and T2/Y2 from the second (line 218 'Q2 = I - Y2 T2 Y2^H'). Independently corroborated by peer-reviewed arXiv:2409.13374 (Eq. 5.19) giving the identical T_new = [[T1, -T1*(Y1^H*Y2)*T2],[0,T2]]. In implementation the −T1(Y1ᴴY2)T2 product is evaluated via a TRMM (unit-lower-triangular top block) + GEMM (rectangular bottom block) split plus TRMM by T1/T2 — a Level-3 construction of T.
findings.confidence_note: Primary LAPACK reference implementation plus peer-reviewed corroboration, unanimous.

findings.claim: For the tiny/per-warp regime (n=32 and within-tile work), QR uniquely favors shared-memory (or a hybrid: registers for storage + shared memory for communication) over a pure register/warp-shuffle implementation — the OPPOSITE of LU and Cholesky — because the inner y = vᵀC matvec in the Householder update needs Q·log₂(N_p2) shuffle-reduction steps (N rounded up to a power of two) versus only P steps with shared memory, where each y element maps to one thread.
findings.evidence: Abdelfattah, Haidar, Tomov, Dongarra (J. Comp. Sci. 26, 2018, the definitive MAGMA/ICL work) states verbatim 'Unlike the Cholesky and LU factorizations, we observe that the shared memory version is faster than the register version, which is the opposite of our initial expectations'; that the update computes 'y = vT C, where C = A[i:N, i+1:N]'; that with shuffles 'the total number of reduction steps is Q×log2(Np2), and not Q×log2(P)'; and 'If both v and C are in shared memory, we can assign each element of y to a single thread... using Q threads, it would take only P steps to find the entire vector y.' Fig.8 shows the hybrid (register storage + shared-memory communication) beats pure shared memory. CAVEAT: this is established only for the tiny/sub-warp regime (matrices size ≤32, one warp per matrix, Pascal/Volta) — it directly informs the contract's n=32 / small per-warp shapes but does NOT transfer to the n=512 blocked regime, where the matrix fits in neither registers nor a single warp.
findings.confidence_note: Peer-reviewed primary source from the authoritative group; mechanism is reduction-arithmetic (architecture-independent), but scope is the tiny-matrix regime only.

findings.claim: A persistent Triton kernel sizes its grid to min(NUM_SMS, total_tiles) — launching at most NUM_SMS programs, each looping over multiple work units — and this structural pattern generalizes from single-matmul tiles to independent problems, making it the attested basis for a persistent one-program-per-matrix batched QR megakernel in the small-n large-batch regime.
findings.evidence: The Triton persistent-matmul tutorial gives verbatim 'grid = lambda META: (min(NUM_SMS, triton.cdiv(M, META["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]) * triton.cdiv(N, META["BLOCK_SIZE_N"])), )' with NUM_SMS = device multi_processor_count, each program looping via 'for tile_id in tl.range(start_pid, num_tiles, NUM_SMS, flatten=True)'. Colfax frames it generally as 'grid fixed to number of SMs ... each CTA persists, processing multiple work units.' Also, for batch ≤ a few thousand one could alternatively launch `batch` programs directly without the min(NUM_SMS,...) cap.

result.caveats:
SCOPE-MATCHED, NOT END-TO-END. The verified claims rigorously establish (a) the compact-WY algebra and the native (H,tau)/R-V packing, (b) the recursive T-assembly recurrence, (c) the shared-memory-vs-shuffle design tradeoff for tiny matrices, and (d) the persistent-Triton grid structure. They do NOT, on their own, constitute a complete recipe for the dominant batch=640/n=512 workload or the FP32-accuracy requirement.

WEAK / CONTESTED AREAS. Several claims central to sub-questions 3, 5, and the large-n part of 4 did NOT survive verification (vote 0-0, 1-0, or were refuted): the explicit three-GEMM trailing-update decomposition (W:=UᴴB, W:=T⁻¹W, B:=B−UW), the T = upper-triangular(UᴴU) diagonal-fixup recipe, the six-Level-3-BLAS DLARFB sequence, and — most importantly for this problem — the SRAM-budget/large-n cooperative-grid bound (the claim that a 512×512 FP32 matrix at 1 MB exceeds 228 KB SRAM and forces a blocked approach was voted 1-2, i.e., net refuted on its specific framing even though the underlying arithmetic is sound). Treat the large-n cooperative-grid necessity as plausible-but-unverified here rather than established.

NO VERIFIED EVIDENCE ON CUTE DSL OR FP32-VIA-TENSOR-CORE. Sub-question 3 (CUTLASS CuTe DSL on sm_100, tcgen05 5th-gen tensor cores) and sub-question 5 (3xTF32 / split-float FP32 emulation, mixed-precision QR with refinement surviving rtol=20·n·eps32 on ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs) produced NO claims that reached the confirmed set. There is therefore no verified guidance on whether TF32/BF16 internal compute can hold FP32 accuracy through the checker on the hard inputs — this is the single biggest correctness risk and is entirely unaddressed by the surviving evidence.

TRIANGLE-SOLVE PRECISION (tau): note that geqrt3-style recursive panels return the compact-WY T factor, not per-reflector tau; matching geqrf exactly requires separately producing tau (the diagonal of the elementary reflectors), which the confirmed claims flag but do not give a kernel-level recipe for.

TIME-SENSITIVITY. The LAPACK/FLAME/Schreiber-Van Loan algebra is timeless. The Triton persistent-kernel APIs (tl.range flatten=True, grid lambda) are 2024-2025 and version-sensitive; verify against the installed Triton on PyTorch 2.11. The MAGMA tiny-matrix finding is on Pascal/Volta and explicitly does not transfer to n=512 on Blackwell.
